objects.description:
Multi-stage Android malware impersonating the mParivahan RTO app, spread via WhatsApp and SMS smishing with shortened URLs. Droppers use ZIP manipulation and native packers; a fake UPI payment flow harvests the UPI PIN, and banking SMS is exfiltrated. Some variants also bundle a cryptominer. 40+ distinct samples observed.

Status in the tracker: active (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2025-09 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Unattributed, financially motivated (Cyble).

Also reported, not expressed as STIX patterns: Telegram bot GhostBatRat_bot.

Infrastructure context, not indicators (legitimate or shared services the campaign abused; do not block): raw.githubusercontent.com; github.com (releases); Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM); Telegram Bot API.

Key findings: A fake ₹1 "ownership verification" UPI screen captures the UPI PIN and sends it to a Firebase endpoint. Banking SMS is exfiltrated and incoming SMS can be forwarded to an attacker number, which hands the operators OTPs and UPI device binding. Payloads are pulled from GitHub; droppers use ZIP-header manipulation and native packers, and terminate on x86 emulators. Device registration runs through a Telegram bot; some variants also run a cryptominer.

One distributor allegedly supplied ~400 fraudsters; linked losses ~Rs 54 lakh. Cash-out via ATM withdrawals left no direct bank trail. No technical IOCs published.

Status in the tracker: law-enforcement (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2026-06 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Arrests by Ahmedabad Cyber Crime Branch (allegations, not yet proven in court).

Key findings: A Telegram bot let buyers purchase, download, swap and renew fraud APKs from impersonation templates. One distributor allegedly supplied the apps to around 400 other fraudsters. Cash-out ran through ATM withdrawals handed over in person, leaving no direct bank trail between buyer and seller.

objects.description:
Hands-on analysis of a sophisticated Android banking trojan spread from a compromised WhatsApp group, using a man-in-the-middle VPN technique and advanced anti-analysis to steal banking credentials. Representative of the higher end of the Android threat targeting Indian users.

Status in the tracker: historical (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2025-10 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Unattributed.

Also reported, not expressed as STIX patterns: Android package com.iudxmm.android.

Key findings: Distributed as 'SBI AADHAR UPDATE.APK' through a WhatsApp group the attacker had taken over and renamed to look official. Shows a fake SBI login page to harvest usernames, passwords and mobile numbers. Routes all device traffic through a malicious VpnService (addRoute 0.0.0.0/0) for man-in-the-middle interception. A malformed ZIP header breaks apktool; no C2 was observed in a sandbox, consistent with anti-sandbox behaviour.

objects.description:
e-Challan / RTO-themed two-stage dropper. A fake 'update' prompt installs a second APK that hides its icon (INFO category), collects Aadhaar/PAN and full card/UPI details via fake payment screens, and intercepts incoming SMS for OTP harvesting. C2 over HTTP POST to jsonserv domains.

Status in the tracker: active (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2025-10 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Unattributed, financially motivated (CYFIRMA).

Key findings: A loader shows a fake "App Update Available" prompt and installs a second APK with the same name and icon. The payload's activity is categorised as INFO rather than LAUNCHER, so it never appears in the app drawer. Fake e-Challan and ₹1 "verification" screens collect Aadhaar, PAN, full card data, ATM PIN, net-banking credentials and UPI PIN; the UPI payment is rigged to fail. Incoming SMS is rebuilt at PDU level and forwarded for OTP theft; C2 is HTTP POST to jsonserv domains with base64-chunked URLs.

objects.description:
Mumbai Cyber Police arrested six members of an interstate syndicate linked to 3,206 complaints on the national portal (~Rs 43 crore). APKs impersonated banks, Mahanagar Gas (MGL) and the RTO; a typical lure warned of a gas disconnection and asked the victim to install an app and pay Rs 10. The apps intercepted OTPs and banking SMS. Forensics found 111 distinct fake APKs; ~8,609 people installed them, and ~1.24 crore SMS were exfiltrated via servers on Google Firebase and Hostinger.

Status in the tracker: law-enforcement (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2026-06 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Arrests by Mumbai Cyber Police (allegations, not yet proven in court).

Infrastructure context, not indicators (legitimate or shared services the campaign abused; do not block): Firebase; Hostinger (web hosting).

Key findings: Linked to 3,206 complaints on the national cyber-crime portal and about Rs 43 crore in losses. Forensics found 111 distinct fake APKs installed by about 8,609 people. About 1.24 crore SMS were exfiltrated to servers on Google Firebase and Hostinger. A typical lure warned of a gas disconnection and asked the victim to install an app and pay Rs 10.

objects.description:
Regional context: one of South Asia's most active APTs, assessed as India-nexus, historically targeting Pakistan, Nepal, China and Afghanistan and more recently expanding to maritime, nuclear and IT sectors across Asia, the Middle East and Africa. Primarily spear-phishing with weaponised documents exploiting known Office flaws. Included here for regional awareness; its targets are largely outside India.

Reported attribution: India-nexus (attributed). Assessed as India-nexus in vendor reporting. Included for regional awareness only; its targets are largely outside India.

Key findings: Kaspersky's March 2025 research: a DOCX uses remote template injection to fetch an RTF that exploits CVE-2017-11882 and delivers Backdoor Loader and StealerBot. Primarily spear-phishing with weaponised documents that exploit known Office flaws. Has expanded from Pakistan, Nepal, China and Afghanistan to maritime, nuclear and IT sectors across Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

objects.name: SideWinder (India-nexus)

objects.description:
A Pakistan-nexus espionage actor that mimics the SideWinder group's TTPs (hence the name) and is widely assessed to overlap with Transparent Tribe/APT36 infrastructure. It targets Indian government, defence and increasingly academic and research institutions. Typical delivery is a ZIP archive embedding an LNK or decoy document that leads to RATs such as ActionRAT, AllaKore and AuTo Stealer, hosted on compromised domains.

Reported attribution: Pakistan-nexus. Linked to the Pakistan-nexus cluster through infrastructure and tooling overlap with Transparent Tribe; the group deliberately mimics SideWinder's TTPs to mislead attribution.

Key findings: The signature chain is a ZIP archive containing an LNK or decoy document that starts a multi-stage infection. Next stages are usually pulled from compromised legitimate websites rather than attacker-registered infrastructure. Payloads rotate between ActionRAT, AllaKore RAT, ReverseRAT and AuTo Stealer, which collects Office files, PDFs, databases and images. Has exploited the WinRAR flaw CVE-2023-38831, where opening a decoy file inside a crafted archive runs the payload, and fielded a Linux variant of Ares RAT (Seqrite, Nov 2023).

objects.name: SideCopy

objects.description:
A long-running espionage actor that primarily targets Indian government, defence and education sectors. Typical tradecraft is spear-phishing with weaponised documents and LNK files, and fake or trojanised apps, delivering RATs such as Crimson RAT, CapraRAT (Android) and Poseidon. 2026 reporting describes new RAT activity, LNK-based delivery chains, and expansion toward India's startup ecosystem.

Reported attribution: Pakistan-nexus. Pakistan-nexus is the consensus of vendor reporting and MITRE ATT&CK. The tracker's confidence rates the evidence for the activity described here, not the attribution.

Key findings: January 2026 campaigns sent a ZIP with an LNK disguised as a PDF; the LNK runs a remote HTA through mshta, which loads the RAT in memory and opens a decoy PDF. February 2026: Acronis TRU attributed, with high confidence, a Crimson RAT campaign against Indian startups, particularly OSINT and cybersecurity firms, delivered as an ISO containing an LNK disguised as an Excel file. Crimson RAT, a .NET RAT delivered through macro documents, remains the workhorse: file theft, screenshots, keylogging and command execution. CapraRAT extends operations to Android through trojanised or fake apps. Delivery has moved from macro documents to OLE and LNK-based chains, with repeated experiments targeting Linux desktops used in Indian government.

objects.description:
China-nexus intrusion sets that have repeatedly targeted India's power sector and critical infrastructure. Recorded Future documented RedEcho targeting Indian electricity load-dispatch centres, and later TAG-38 activity against grid infrastructure in Ladakh using the ShadowPad backdoor and compromised internet-facing DVR/IoT devices for C2. A reminder that the threat to India isn't only fraud and Pakistan-nexus espionage.

Reported attribution: China-nexus. China-nexus per Recorded Future's RedEcho and TAG-38 reporting. Confidence is medium because the public record rests largely on one vendor's analysis.

Key findings: RedEcho (disclosed February 2021) targeted Indian power-sector organisations, including regional load-dispatch centres, using the ShadowPad backdoor. TAG-38 (disclosed April 2022) targeted grid infrastructure in Ladakh, using compromised internet-facing DVR/IoT devices in its command-and-control path. Activity has coincided with periods of India-China border tension, consistent with collection and pre-positioning.

objects.description:
Analyst assessment by Sohan Kanna: judgement over the tracker's feeds, not source-reported fact.

The Indian threat picture this month is pulled in two directions at once: high-volume, financially-motivated mobile fraud hitting citizens at scale, and patient, state-aligned intrusion aimed at government, defence and critical infrastructure. The common seam is the edge — VPNs, firewalls and cloud identity — which is where ransomware crews and espionage actors alike still get their first foothold.

1. Fake-APK UPI fraud has gone industrial (critical): This is no longer lone scammers. Organised networks now run fake RTO / e-challan, bank and utility APKs end to end: a single Mumbai bust was linked to 3,206 complaints and roughly ₹43 crore, and Ahmedabad police separately broke up a Telegram storefront that sold the apps to about 400 fraudsters. Individual losses keep surfacing too, such as two Pune residents who lost over ₹14 lakh to the same e-challan lure. Cash-out is fast and hard to trace (ATM withdrawals in the Ahmedabad case), and the malware (GhostBat RAT and kin) intercepts OTPs and banking SMS and captures the UPI PIN through a fake payment screen. For any payments operator, this is the live, high-volume threat, not a future one.

2. The edge is still the way in (high): The India-relevant watchlist is dominated by internet-facing edge: Ivanti Connect Secure, Citrix NetScaler, PAN-OS and Fortinet, plus SharePoint (CVE-2025-53770, EPSS ~100%, ransomware-linked). These are the products Indian enterprises expose to the internet, and CISA lists known ransomware use for several of them, from Ivanti (CVE-2025-22457) and NetScaler (CVE-2025-5777) to PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0257) and FortiOS (CVE-2024-55591). If you do one thing this month, make it edge patch cadence: it is the single highest-leverage control on this list.

3. Pakistan-nexus espionage is persistent, not episodic (high): Transparent Tribe (APT36) and SideCopy continue to target Indian government, defence, education and research with Crimson RAT and the ZIP→LNK→LOLBin delivery pattern. These are not one-off campaigns; they are a standing collection effort that re-tools faster than it disappears. If you sit in gov, defence or academia, assume you are in scope and detect for the delivery chain, not just the final implant.

4. Identity is the new perimeter: watch M365 sign-ins (medium-high): Microsoft and the UK NCSC reported in April 2026 that Forest Blizzard (APT28) changed DNS settings on compromised home and small-office routers to put adversary-in-the-middle servers in front of Outlook on the web, where passwords and login tokens can be intercepted. As Indian organisations move onto M365 / Entra, staff home routers become part of the attack surface. Entra sign-in risk is the signal to wire up first; Microsoft's guidance points to its risky sign-in detections. The tracker's Entra rule (high-risk successful sign-in) and its endpoint DNS rule are complementary investigation leads, not a detection of this chain: they fire separately and are not correlated, the Entra rule does not verify the MFA sequence, and a hijacked router hands out its resolver through DHCP, which the endpoint DNS rule deliberately ignores. Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys / FIDO2) is the control that breaks the relay.

5. China-nexus pre-positioning in the power sector (medium): RedEcho's targeting of load dispatch centres is about access held for later, not immediate disruption — lower tempo, higher stakes. This is the kind of intrusion that matters in a crisis rather than a quarterly report, and it belongs on the radar of anyone defending Indian critical infrastructure even when nothing is visibly happening.

objects.description: Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway Out-of-Bounds Read Vulnerability. Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway contain an out-of-bounds read vulnerability due to insufficient input validation. In CISA KEV since 2025-07-10, with known ransomware use.

objects.name: CVE-2024-55591

objects.description: Microsoft SharePoint Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability. Microsoft SharePoint Server on-premises contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability that could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. This vulnerability could be chained with CVE-2025-53771. CVE-2025-53770 is a patch bypass for CVE-2025-49704, and the updates for CVE-2025-53770 include more robust protection than those for CVE-2025-49704. In CISA KEV since 2025-07-20, with known ransomware use.
